chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Musa ibn Umar from Abdullah ibn al-Mughira from al-Subbah al-Muzani who said:
The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said: 'Fifty-nine (95) takbirs in the day and night for the prayers, including the takbir of the qunut.'

Thus, these narrations include mention of the takbir added to the qunut in a general manner and in a detailed manner, and they also include the number of takbirs as ninety-five. And if there were no takbir in the qunut, the takbirs would have been ninety.
And no one should say that I interpret the excess over ninety takbirs as meaning that when the pray-er rises from the first tashahhud to the third, he stands with a takbir.

For three reasons: the first is that not all prayers involve rising from the second rak'ah to the third, and this is only present in four prayers. So if that were the intended meaning, he would have said ninety-four takbirs.

The second is that the detailed hadith includes mention of eleven takbirs in the morning prayer (al-Ghada), and the takbir of the qunut is added to it. And if the matter were as they said, the takbir in it would be only eleven takbirs.
The third is that many narrations have come stating that it is appropriate for a person to rise from the first tashahhud to the third saying: 'By the power and strength of Allah, I rise and I sit.'

So if rising with the takbir were obligatory, he would say: 'Then he takbirs and rises to the third.' Just as when they mentioned the bowing and prostration, they said: 'Then he takbirs and bows, and takbirs and prostrates, and raises his head from prostration and takbirs.'
So if there were a takbir here, he would say the same. And that is what we have narrated.
ai.seo_question: How many takbirs are performed in daily prayers according to Shia jurisprudence, and where are they located?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam Ali (AS) establishes the total of ninety-five takbirs in daily prayers, with the scholar clarifying that the excess over ninety is attributed to the Qunut supplication rather than rising between rak'ahs. The text refutes alternative interpretations by citing specific narrations regarding the eleven takbirs in Fajr prayer and the standard ritual phrasing for movements, thereby solidifying the Shia jurisprudential stance on the precise enumeration of prayer actions.
